parts.name: Google Coral USB Accelerator / Edge TPU
parts.host_requirements: Debian Linux, macOS or Windows host; TensorFlow Lite Edge TPU model path
parts.software_stack: TensorFlow Lite / Edge TPU compiler / PyCoral / libedgetpu
parts.plain_language: Coral is useful precisely because it is not an LLM accelerator. A roughly 2W TPU can absorb fixed INT8 vision/classification jobs so the expensive Ryzen or GenAI accelerator stays free for language work. The router should treat this as a specialist, never as a general transformer node.
parts.source_notes: Coral lists US$59.99, 4 TOPS INT8 and 2 TOPS per watt. The software path is TensorFlow Lite Edge TPU, not a general LLM runtime.

parts.name: MemryX MX3 M.2 AI Accelerator, 4-chip module
parts.host_requirements: x86, Arm or RISC-V host with compatible PCIe/M.2 and MSI-X support
parts.plain_language: MX3 is another example of why the cluster should route by workload instead of forcing everything through an LLM node. Its tiny at-memory accelerator chips are excellent candidates for continuous vision pipelines, but their small on-chip model storage makes them a poor fit for billion-parameter language models.
parts.source_notes: MemryX documentation describes a four-MX3 M.2 module, with each chip typically using 0.5-3W. MemryX published an around-US$150 module reference in 2026 and separately describes roughly 5W typical / 10W TDP for the four-chip module.

parts.name: Intel Neural Compute Stick 2 / Myriad X EOL reference
parts.plain_language: NCS2 is deliberately kept as an EOL reference. It may appear cheaply on the used market and can still offload old OpenVINO vision workloads, but its frozen software track and limited model class make it a poor target for new LLM deployment. Tracking it teaches the catalog how to say “cheap but obsolete.”
parts.source_notes: Intel marks NCS2 discontinued; OpenVINO support is maintained on the 2022.3.x LTS track. No current used price is recorded.
